title: The Songbook of the Old Mill House
premise: Kestrel Pemberton, a once-celebrated cellist whose hands froze mid-concert, retreats to the Old Mill House on a tidal island to rebuild his discipline and bury his stage fright. When his family descends for a reunion, he hires local ferryman and amateur songwriter Wren Calloway to pose as his boyfriend — a transactional arrangement that curdles into something neither can name. As Kestrel's estranged mother pushes him toward one last comeback audition in London, Wren's own unfinished songs force him to confront that hiding behind technique was never living. At the season's final ferry, Kestrel must choose between the career that once defined him and the man who heard his silence as music; he stays, plays an unscripted cello set at the mill house, and begins composing with Wren instead of performing for strangers.
about_author: N. M. Eriksen is the pen name of a former orchestral librarian who spent a decade cataloguing other people's music before writing love stories set where the tide decides the schedule. They live on a coastal island much like the one in this book, where the last ferry of the season is a genuine annual heartbreak.

chapters.title: The Ferry That Waits
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Arriving at the Old Mill House with a broken career and a rehearsed smile, Kestrel rehearses excuses for the reunion until he meets Wren, who fixes boats and hums melodies he never finishes. A desperate bargain is struck over engine grease and tea: Wren will play the devoted boyfriend for one weekend. The beat is guarded hope disguised as practicality.

chapters.title: Duet for Two Liars
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The reunion weekend unfolds in staged hand-holding and improvised history, but the lies grow tender: Wren shares a half-written song about leaving, and Kestrel's mother probes the 'relationship' with surgical suspicion. By dessert, the fake date feels devastatingly real, and both men realize they've stopped acting. The beat is intimacy arriving through pretense.

chapters.title: What the Tide Takes Back
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Kestrel's London audition offer arrives by letter, and his mother reveals she engineered it, exposing cracks in the fake romance. Wren, who has watched everyone he loves leave on the last ferry, withdraws before he can be abandoned first. Kestrel plays cello alone at midnight for the first time since the catastrophe — not flawlessly, but honestly. The beat is rupture and raw self-recognition.

chapters.title: The Last Crossing
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. On the morning of the final ferry, Kestrel stands at the dock with a ticket in one hand and Wren's unfinished songbook in the other. He lets the boat go, walks back to the mill house, and plays the song through to its ending while Wren listens from the doorway. They finish it together. The beat is belonging chosen over performance.
